newsitem.title: ITALY: Hearing for Italian PM adjourned for six weeks.
newsitem.headline: Hearing for Italian PM adjourned for six weeks.

text.p: A committal hearing to decide if Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi should stand trial for alleged abuse of office and conflict of interest opened on Wednesday and was adjourned until February 28.
Prodi denies the charges, which relate to a controversial sale by state holding company IRI in October 1993 when he was chairman, and says he will not resign over the affair.

Prosecutor Giuseppa Geremia alleges that Prodi and five other IRI board members at the time awarded an "unjust advantage" to a little-known southern Italian consortium, Fis.Vi., in its purchase of food company Cirio.

Prodi's lawyer Paola Severino told reporters that presiding judge Edoardo Landi took just 40 minutes to decide on the adjournment, conceded at the request of a defence lawyer now engaged in another trial.
Prodi did not attend the hearing and only one of the accused was present for the brief closed-door session in Rome's main court building.

"We were ready to discuss our aspects of the case as of today but the reasons for a delay were well-founded. February 28 was the date all lawyers were available so we will continue then," Severino said.
Prodi, who has headed a centre-left coalition since last May, has suffered no evident political damage from the case, which does not involve any allegations of personal enrichment.
Public reaction has been negligible, especially when compared to public outrage stirred by the corruption cases of the early 1990s which toppled Italy's old political class.
The offence of abuse of office can be levelled against state employees and has itself become controversial, with President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro joining calls for a change in the law.
Critics of the charge argue that it is vague, ranging in potential scope from administrative errors that would not constitute a criminal offence in many countries to bad business practice to fraud.
Cirio, best known for its canned tomatoes, was sold privately to Fis.Vi. after IRI decided that offers submitted in a public tender did not meet the right conditions.
Fis.Vi soon after sold the food company's olive oil interests to the Anglo-Dutch group Unilever, for which Prodi had worked as a consultant, and has since divested itself of the whole group.
Prodi denies his relationship with Unilever held any conflict of interest, saying he had cut his ties months earlier, in May 1993, when he became chairman of IRI for a second time.
